newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaireans block aid delivery to Rwandan Hutu camps.
newsitem.headline: Zaireans block aid delivery to Rwandan Hutu camps.

text.p: Hundreds of angry Zaireans stopped aid workers reaching teeming Rwandan Hutu refugee camps on Friday, posing new problems for a delayed U.N. repatriation plan, witnesses said.
The demonstrators prevented an aid convoy from disembarking a Zaire river ferry, attacking vehicles and threatening aid workers in a protest over the refugees and the aid they receive.
The demonstrators told Reuters the refugees should move deeper into the jungle away from Kisangani, Zaire's third city. They said they did not want Western aid workers crossing the river.
"The Zairean population refuses to let the whites (aid officials) take food to the refugees because the refugees are killing local Zaireans," said Yenga Masomboye, a boat operator.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said the incident was a setback but that it hoped to get into the camp soon.

The United Nations delayed an operation set to start on Friday to repatriate the first batch of 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees after rebel officials expressed fear that it could spread cholera in the region.

"We are optimistic that they (regional authorities) will conclude that this is safe to do and that we will be able to start on Saturday," UNHCR regional spokesman Paul Stromberg told reporters in Kisangani on Thursday.
A total of 330 cholera cases and 19 cholera deaths have been recorded at Kasese refugee camp, 25 km (16 miles) south of Kisangani, according to U.N. figures.
Around 100,000 sick and exhausted Rwandan refugees arrived near a railway line south of Kisangani last month begging to go home after a five-month trek through the jungle.

Rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, led by Laurent kabila, control nearly half of Zaire after a six-month campaign to oust ailing president Mobutu Sese Seko, Zaire's ruler since 1965.

The rebels say armed Hutus among the refugees from the former Rwandan government army and extremist Interahamwe militia who played a leading role in the 1994 Rwandan genocide pose a grave security threat.
Newly elected governor Yagi Sitolo told Reuters he feared cholera could spread if refugees were brought to Kisangani airport for the flight home.
Senior aid officials planned to meet regional authorities on Friday in an effort to convince them the repatriation posed no threat, Stromberg said.

U.N. agencies and non-governmental organisations are nursing the refugees back to health and UNHCR has devised a multi-million dollar plan to take the refugees on trucks, planes and barges across the Zaire river back to Rwanda.
Eighty healthy but unaccompanied Rwandan children were to be flown to the eastern town of Goma on Friday at the start of the opeation.
More than a million Hutu refugees fled eastern Zaire camps at the start of the rebel campaign. Most returned to Rwanda in November but hundreds of thousands more fled deeper into Zaire.
